transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2026-03-04
Time: 10:00 AM PT
Duration: 30 minutes
Attendees: Samir (Redwood AE), Ava (Redwood SE), Michael (CTO, Stonebridge), Laura (Head of Data), Evan (Infra)

Auto Summary: Discovery to align on cost/unit economics across Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private. Customer provided rough traffic profile; Redwood team outlined pricing levers and suggested a benchmark.

[00:00] Samir (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. Quick intros - I'm Samir, AE, and Ava is our SE.
[00:12] Michael (Stonebridge): Hi, Michael here. Laura and Evan on my side. Appreciate the time.
[00:20] Ava (Redwood SE): Great - goal for today is to understand your workload and walk through how batching, caching, and reserved capacity change unit costs. We can sketch an initial cost model.
[00:33] Laura (Stonebridge): Perfect. High level: we're building an internal research assistant for our analysts, mixed retrieval + generation. Avg prompt length is around 150 tokens, responses ~600 tokens; so ballpark 750 tokens per transaction. Expected volume is 1.2M transactions/month in peak, but initially 200k/mo ramping to 1M over 6 months. Latency SLO is p95 under 800ms for interactive flows.
[01:00] Evan (Infra): We also care about isolation - some models need to run in a VPC or dedicated pool because of compliance.
[01:12] Samir: Got it. Two axes we'll consider: cost per token and latency/throughput. Hosted gives easiest onboarding and per-token pricing; Dedicated reduces unit cost with reserved GPU capacity and better tail latency, Private adds control but comes with platform + infra costs.
[01:35] Michael: Can you give a rough worked example - like cost per million tokens for hosted vs dedicated assuming our numbers?
[01:42] Ava: Sure, quick back-of-envelope. With hosted generation pricing, assume ~ $X per 1k tokens at baseline (note: we'll send exact numbers in the sheet). For your 750 tokens/request and 200k requests, that's 150M tokens/month. With naive hosted pricing that maps to T dollars - but important: batching and prefix/KV caching change the effective tokens sent to the model and GPU utilization.
[02:10] Michael: OK, let's talk about caching - what are the realistic savings?
[02:15] Ava: Two main levers: prefix/prompt caching (if many queries share similar context) and KV cache reuse for assistant-style sessions. For a research assistant we often see 1.5x-3x effective reduction in per-token compute from cache reuse depending on re-use patterns. Continuous batching can also raise GPU throughput, lowering $/token by up to 2-4x compared to single-request latencies, but that comes with tradeoffs for tail latency.
[02:44] Laura: So if we have lots of repeated retrieval/context, we might see a 2x drop?
[02:48] Ava: Yes, that's common. If users re-use documents or prompts, prefix caching avoids recomputing early layers. We'll instrument with your prompt set to estimate more precisely.
[02:59] Evan: How about quantization - you mentioned 4-bit earlier?
[03:03] Ava: Right. Quantization to 4-bit or 8-bit reduces memory footprint and lets us fit larger batches on a GPU. Typical throughput gains are model and architecture dependent. For many Llama-type models, 4-bit can be nearly equivalent in quality for generation tasks and can reduce infrastructure cost by enabling higher utilization. We'll include a quant comparison in the benchmark.
[03:25] Michael: Any tradeoffs on latency for batching? Our p95 needs are strict.
[03:30] Ava: Continuous batching increases throughput but introduces small queuing latency. For p95 under 800ms we can configure smaller batch windows and still get decent GPU utilization; Dedicated gives more control over batch sizes and tail latency.
[03:45] Samir: Important commercial note - Dedicated is reserved capacity: you commit to a pool (monthly/annual). At full utilization that reduces the $/token materially versus hosted. Hosted is good if you want variable usage with no commit. Private adds platform fee + infra ops overhead.
[04:03] Michael: Can you quantify 'materially'? I know numbers vary but any example percent reduction?
[04:08] Ava: As a rule of thumb we've seen reserved/committed capacity reduce unit costs by ~30-60% depending on utilization and model. If you can sustain steady throughput at high utilization, dedicated wins. If usage is spiky and unpredictable, hosted plus burst handling might be simpler.
[04:23] Laura: What about burst? If we commit but need to spike higher, is there an easy burst option?
[04:29] Samir: Yes - we offer burst capacity on top of reserved pools for hosted bursts or over-provisioning within Dedicated with pay-as-you-go for the spike. There's also automated routing to slightly cheaper fallback model variants if you want to optimize costs during spikes.
[04:45] Evan: Security - private control plane? KMS? SOC2?
[04:48] Ava: We support VPC peering, private control plane, and KMS integrations. Redwood Private includes a customer-managed control plane option for on-prem or VPC deployments. We have SOC 2 Type II and can share our security pack.
[04:59] Michael: Great. Back to numbers - can you walk through a concrete example using our low-volume and target-volume?
[05:05] Ava: Quick calc: 750 tokens/req x 200k req = 150M tokens. If hosted is hypothetically $0.02 per 1k tokens (we'll replace with exact), that's ~ $3k for 150M tokens? - wait let me compute, sorry, math flub, 150M tokens is 150,000 * 1k tokens, so at $0.02 per 1k that's $3,000. But that's simplistic. If caching reduces compute 2x, effective tokens billable might be 75M -> $1,500. Dedicated might lower the $/1k to $0.008 at high utilization leading to $1,200 for 150M. The point is the knobs can flip economics by multiple factors.
[06:02] Michael: That math helps, thanks. We need the exact pricing to make a decision.
[06:06] Samir: We'll send a detailed spreadsheet showing hosted per-1k numbers, dedicated reservation tiers and the math to run scenarios with your exact traffic. Also we'll include model variants and quantized options.
[06:18] Laura: For the pilot, what's the recommended scope? Dedicated pilot or hosted benchmark?
[06:22] Ava: Start with hosted benchmark to validate output quality quickly. If you want to test latency and tail behavior under dedicated-style conditions, we can spin a short dedicated cluster for the benchmark. For compliance-sensitive models we'll run benchmarks inside a VPC/dedicated pool.
[06:37] Evan: For Private, what's the cost profile? Is it platform licensing plus infra?
[06:40] Samir: Correct - Private includes a one-time/on-going platform fee plus optionally annual support. Then you'll pay for infra (your GPUs/hosts) and we can provide the software bundle. For some customers with strict residency and audit requirements Private still makes sense despite higher TCO.
[06:56] Michael: Anything else we should consider re: tokenization differences? We've got retrieval that sometimes expands tokens a lot.
[07:02] Ava: Tokenization and system prompt size matter; our cost model accounts for prompt + response tokens. For retrieval-heavy workloads, you can pre-truncate or chunk retrieval docs and rely on reranking to reduce unnecessary tokenization. We'll review your prompt set to find quick wins.
[07:20] Laura: Who owns the KV cache? Is it customer data?
[07:23] Samir: In Hosted, cached items tied to your account are isolated and not used for other customers. For Private you fully control cache storage. We can map out retention/eviction policies.
[07:36] Michael: Competitors? We were also benchmarking Bedrock and Anthropic.
[07:40] Samir: Totally expected. We can include comparative unit economics and latency numbers where available, but direct benchmarks are the best method since models and infra vary.
[07:50] Laura: Ok next steps?
[07:52] Samir: Recap: we'll send pricing sheet and a modeled example for your 200k and 1.2M cases, Ava will run benchmarks including quantization comparison and caching estimates, Michael will send prompt set and traffic profile, then we'll reconvene after benchmarks.
[08:08] Michael: Sounds good. Anything on contract terms if we go Dedicated? Commit lengths?
[08:12] Samir: Standard monthly and annual reserves - longer commits get better unit pricing. We can show breakout in the pricing sheet. Also add-on SLAs for uptime/latency if needed.
[08:24] Evan: For the benchmark, do you need us to share any keys or sample data?
[08:28] Ava: We'll need a sample prompt set and representative data. For compliance-sensitive items you can anonymize or run the benchmark in your VPC.
[08:38] Michael: We'll aim to share materials by Friday.
[08:42] Samir: Awesome - we'll follow up with calendar invite for the benchmark kickoff and the cost model. Thanks everyone.

Meeting Recap (auto): Keys: 1) Host vs Dedicated economics depend on utilization and caching, 2) Caching + quantization may reduce unit cost by multiple factors, 3) Next steps include pricing sheet and benchmark run.

[08:58] End of call.
